questions.prompt: What main difference does this chapter draw between praise and flattery?
choices: Praise is public while flattery is private
Praise sounds observed and believable, while flattery makes motive too audible
Praise is brief while flattery is always long

explanation.gentle: Right. The chapter says positive words gain power when they feel credible instead of oily.
explanation.direct: The distinction is credibility. Praise sounds observed and socially believable. Flattery exposes agenda.
explanation.competitive: If motive gets louder than the observation, the compliment turns on you.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter give so much attention to indirect praise?
choices: Because praise is only powerful when the other person never hears it directly
Because compliments can sound cleaner when they travel through context or other people instead of blunt self-serving delivery
Because indirectness helps you hide what you really think of someone

explanation.gentle: Exactly. Indirect recognition can sound more believable because it carries less visible agenda.
explanation.direct: The chapter is not worshipping indirection. It is showing why social travel and implication can make admiration sound cleaner.
explanation.competitive: Compliments often land harder when they do not look like bids for immediate return.

questions.prompt: What makes a small compliment stronger than a big gush in this chapter?
choices: It is more specific and better proportioned to what was actually observed
It uses fewer emotional words so nobody can question it
It avoids naming any real trait or action directly

explanation.gentle: Yes. A small exact line often carries more trust than a large speech built on thin observation.
explanation.direct: The chapter values proportion. Weight should come from accuracy, not from compliment volume.
explanation.competitive: Big praise with weak evidence smells like leverage. Small praise with strong evidence lands hard.

questions.prompt: Helena wants to recognize a coworker after a difficult meeting. Which move best fits the chapter?
choices: Tell the coworker they are amazing in every possible way so the support feels generous
Name the specific calm or judgment the coworker showed under pressure
Wait until other people leave so the compliment feels more secret and therefore more sincere

explanation.gentle: Helena helps most by naming the real quality she actually saw in the moment.
explanation.direct: Specific, observed praise carries more credibility than broad admiration with weak evidence.
explanation.competitive: Point at the exact trait that earned the respect instead of flooding the room with cheap volume.

questions.prompt: Victor compliments a student leader so intensely at a banquet that the room goes tight. What likely happened?
choices: He gave too little praise for the setting
His admiration got louder than the observation supporting it
He should have delivered the same message through a friend instead

explanation.gentle: Good catch. The chapter warns that praise can embarrass or cheapen when intensity outruns credibility.
explanation.direct: The room tightened because the compliment started sounding like pressure instead of recognition.
explanation.competitive: He spent more admiration than the evidence could cash.

questions.prompt: What does Boomeranging add beyond praising the visible act itself?
choices: It reflects the valued trait behind the act back to the person
It redirects praise so the speaker looks humble
It turns compliments into a joke so they feel lighter

explanation.gentle: Exactly. Boomeranging names the quality the act revealed, not only the act itself.
explanation.direct: The chapter says identity-level praise can stay with people longer because it affirms what kind of person they seemed to be.
explanation.competitive: Surface praise rewards the move. Boomeranging rewards the person who made it.

questions.prompt: Sumi gives repeated little strokes over time instead of one giant compliment. Why can that work better here?
choices: Because repeated, specific affirmation can feel more believable than a single oversized speech
Because people stop noticing praise after the first compliment anyway
Because small praise is always safer than direct praise in every setting

explanation.gentle: The chapter likes small, credible reinforcement because it can feel more natural and less loaded.
explanation.direct: Little strokes work when they accumulate observed recognition without sounding like a performance event.
explanation.competitive: Steady believable praise often carries more weight than one dramatic dump of admiration.

questions.prompt: What is the point of the Tombstone Game in this chapter?
choices: It asks what quality would feel durably true enough to be worth remembering
It teaches you to make compliments sound darker and more dramatic
It suggests that legacy language should replace all ordinary praise

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter uses that frame to reach beyond surface shine toward lasting character.
explanation.direct: Legacy-frame praise has force because it names a trait that feels more enduring than a momentary success.
explanation.competitive: If the quality would still matter years later, the praise gains unusual weight.

questions.prompt: What is the clearest marker that praise has slipped into flattery?
choices: When the listener can hear your motive more clearly than your observation
When the compliment names a trait instead of an action
When you praise someone more than once in the same month

explanation.gentle: That is the warning. Praise fails when it starts feeling like social handling instead of truthful recognition.
explanation.direct: Flattery begins when agenda outruns credibility. The observation no longer feels like the real center of the compliment.
explanation.competitive: The move flips the second leverage gets louder than truth.

questions.prompt: After admiration works in person, which channel changes the rules by taking the face away?
choices: How to remove praise from relationships so motive never gets questioned
How these social signals change when only voice, timing, and the phone line remain
How to make every compliment travel indirectly through other people

explanation.gentle: That is the next step. The book shifts from praise in person to how connection works when the face disappears.
explanation.direct: Chapter 7 naturally follows by asking how social intelligence changes on the phone, where voice and timing do more of the work.
explanation.competitive: Once the face is gone, the signal has to ride on voice alone.
